Caspian anadromous shad (Alosa kessleri) is a pelagic-zone clupeid that undertakes extensive spawning migrations from the Caspian Sea into major river systems such as the Volga and Ural. This species exhibits a maximum total length that ranks among the highest recorded for the genus, reaching up to 52 centimeters [Li = up to 52 centimeters] in older individuals, a size that reflects the productive foraging conditions available in the southern Caspian basin. The total length at which the onset of gonadal activity becomes detectable is approximately 38 centimeters [Lp = approximately 38 centimeters], marking the transition from the immature juvenile phase to the early stages of reproductive competence. Field surveys conducted in the lower Volga delta indicate that individuals attaining this size are typically between two and three years of age, suggesting a relatively prolonged period of somatic growth before reproductive effort is initiated. The length-based estimate of the wet weight at puberty, derived from length-weight regressions fitted to locally captured specimens, yields a value of 591 grams [Wwp = 591 grams], a body mass that implies substantial accumulation of lipid reserves, likely necessary to sustain the energetic demands of the upstream migration and subsequent gamete production.

The wet weight at birth for this species, corresponding to the newly fertilized ovum following water hardening, is approximately 0.0042 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0042 grams], a value that aligns closely with the egg diameters of 1.7 to 2.4 millimeters reported for the congeneric Alosa fallax. These transparent, pelagic eggs are carried by river currents during the early incubation period, and their modest individual mass facilitates widespread dispersal of the progeny. The ultimate wet weight attained by fully grown adults, calculated from length-weight relationships applied to the maximum recorded total length, is estimated at 1557 grams [Wwi = 1557 grams], placing Alosa kessleri among the heavier-bodied representatives of the genus within the Ponto-Caspian region. This adult body mass is achieved through a growth trajectory that appears to decelerate markedly after individuals reach approximately 38 centimeters in length, with resources thereafter increasingly directed toward gonadal maturation and the maintenance of body condition during the fasting period of spawning migration.

Reproductive output in Caspian anadromous shad is characterized by a pronounced seasonal peak aligned with spring river temperatures. At the thermal optimum of 10.8 °C [T = 10.8 °C], which typifies the water conditions during the main spawning run in the lower Volga, gravid females produce an estimated total clutch of approximately 312000 eggs [N_R_i = clutch of approximately 312000 eggs] and typically accomplish a single spawning event each year [F_R_i = single spawning event each year]. This annual reproductive strategy, involving a single, large clutch deposited during a brief spawning window, is consistent with the life-history pattern of a migratory iteroparous clupeid that experiences a period of intensive feeding in marine waters prior to the riverine spawning migration. The extremely high fecundity offsets the high rates of egg and larval mortality inherent to a pelagic early-life strategy, in which both the free-floating eggs and the tiny yolk-sac larvae are vulnerable to predation and advective loss from suitable nursery habitats.

A comprehensive mark-recapture study conducted over eleven consecutive years in the Volga River estuary provided reliable data on the longevity of Alosa kessleri under natural conditions. The oldest documented individual, a female recovered near the spawning grounds, had a lifespan of 2920 days [am = 2920 days], which corresponds to approximately eight calendar years at a temperature of 10.8 °C [T = 10.8 °C]. This record was established in an environment where the mean annual water temperature during the growing season averages 10.8 °C [T = 10.8 °C], a thermal regime that likely constrains annual metabolic expenditure and contributes to the species' moderately extended lifespan relative to smaller, short-lived clupeids. The longevity data indicate that the population includes multiple age classes, providing demographic stability and opportunities for repeated spawning across several seasons. Senescent changes, including reduced fecundity and declining body condition, become apparent in the oldest age classes, consistent with the progressive physiological deterioration observed in other long-lived migratory teleosts reaching the terminal phase of their life cycle. Mortality rates increase sharply after the seventh year, suggesting a senescent phase.

Comparative growth analysis of congeneric shads within the Alosa genus reveals that Caspian anadromous shad follows a trajectory that is intermediate between the slow-growing, longer-lived Alosa saposhnikovi and the faster-maturing, shorter-lived Alosa caspia. The length at puberty of 38 centimeters [Lp = 38 centimeters] represents approximately 73 percent of the ultimate total length of 52 centimeters [Li = 52 centimeters], a proportional value that is consistent with the pattern observed in other moderately iteroparous migratory clupeids. The corresponding wet weight at puberty of 591 grams [Wwp = 591 grams] is reached when the fish have accumulated roughly 38 percent of their ultimate wet body mass of 1557 grams [Wwi = 1557 grams], indicating that a substantial portion of adult mass gain occurs after the onset of reproductive maturity. This post-maturity growth, combined with the extreme fecundity of approximately 312000 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 312000 eggs per year] when spawning at 10.8 °C [T = 10.8 °C], suggests a life-history strategy that balances continued somatic investment against the high immediate reproductive output necessary for population persistence in a variable estuarine environment.
